# What Are These Hoses That Are Sticking Out?

If you are looking at a 2008 Honda Hornet CB600F and seeing two hoses protruding near the gear shifter, you aren't dealing with a custom modification or a mysterious aftermarket add-on. You are likely observing a factory-installed component that has simply moved from its intended resting position. One of these lines connects directly to the coolant reservoir located under the seat; the other traces back to the engine block before disappearing into the chassis cavity where it was originally secured.

The confusion usually stems from the specific routing found on this generation of CB600F models. The thicker hose you identified is indeed a coolant overflow return line. It connects the upper expansion tank to the radiator or the lower section of the cooling circuit depending on the exact service manual revision for your specific year. In modern automotive and motorcycle engineering, this isn't just about "overflow" in the sense of boiling over during overheating. The system relies on thermal expansion. As the engine heats up, the coolant volume increases. This excess fluid needs a place to go without pressurizing the system to dangerous levels or forcing it out through the radiator cap prematurely. When the engine cools down and contracts, that same reservoir feeds back into the main cooling loop, maintaining proper fill levels automatically.

The second hose, which you found difficult to trace, is often part of the same assembly or a separate vacuum line routed in close proximity due to chassis design constraints. On many 2008 Hornets, wiring harnesses and smaller fluid lines are routed through tight channels near the swingarm pivot and shifter linkage. Over time, vibration and heat cycling can cause these lines to loosen their retaining clips or slide out of their molded tracks. Once unsecured, gravity pulls them toward the lowest point in the area, which is often right next to the gear lever.

If you are inspecting this setup, check for a small plastic clip or a rubber grommet that anchors the hose end near the shifter tunnel. If that anchor is missing or broken, the hose will dangle freely. While it may look alarming to see fluid lines exposed in an open chassis area, leaving them disconnected poses a significant risk. A dangling overflow hose can eventually snag on the drive chain, gear lever, or footpegs. A single instance of catching on the chain could tear the hose, leading to coolant loss and potential engine overheating.

From a maintenance perspective, the decision to re-secure these hoses is straightforward but critical. You do not need to replace them immediately unless there are signs of cracks, brittleness, or active weeping at the connection points. However, finding the original mounting point is essential. Referencing the service manual for the CB600F will show you that there are often specific guides molded into the frame rails designed to hold these lines in place. Re-installing them into their designated tracks prevents future interference with moving parts and keeps the routing clean.

If you cannot locate the original mounting point after cleaning the area, using a high-quality zip tie or a new rubber grommet is an acceptable interim solution, provided it does not introduce sharp edges that could damage the hose insulation. Always ensure the coolant level in the reservoir is correct before riding, as air pockets introduced during a loose connection can lead to false temperature readings on your gauge.
